Vice Premier of China :: Selection :: chunk_0010
Officially, the vice premiers are appointed by the [National People's Congress](/wiki/National_People%27s_Congress "National People's Congress") (NPC) upon the nomination of the premier.[[4]](#cite_note-:023-4) The NPC also has the power to remove the vice premiers and other state officers from office. Elections and removals are decided by majority vote.[[4]](#cite_note-:023-4) In practice, the vice premiers are chosen within the [Chinese Communist Party](/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party") (CCP) leadership, including the Politburo Standing Committee.[[5]](#cite_note-:82-5) Candidates for top positions including the vice premier are first approved first by the CCP's Politburo Standing Committee, and then by its [Politburo](/wiki/Politburo_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "Politburo of the Chinese Communist Party"), then approved in a special plenary session the Central Committee just before the NPC session for vote by the Congress, with the premier nominating the candidates during the NPC session.[[6]](#cite_note-:822-6)

The length of the vice premier's term of office is the same as the NPC, which is 5 years, and the vice premiers are restricted to two consecutive terms.[[4]](#cite_note-:023-4) Immediately after the election, the [president](/wiki/President_of_China "President of China") signs the presidential order formalizing the appointment of the vice premiers. Since 2018, the vice premiers are required to collectively [recite](/wiki/Recitation "Recitation") the [constitutional oath of office](/wiki/Constitutional_oath_of_office_of_China "Constitutional oath of office of China") before assuming office.[[5]](#cite_note-:82-5)

Alcohol and cancer :: Mechanisms :: Local carcinogenic effect of ethanol :: chunk_0007
The risk of cancer associated with alcohol consumption is higher in tissues in closest contact on ingestion of alcohol, such as the oral cavity, pharynx and esophagus. This is explained by the fact that ethanol is a proven [carcinogen](/wiki/Carcinogen "Carcinogen") and in addition, [metabolite](/wiki/Metabolite "Metabolite") of ethanol (acetaldehyde) produced in the liver is highly carcinogenic, thus explaining both local (mouth, throat, esophageal cancers) as well as distant (skin, liver, breast) cancers. It is well known that [ethanol](/wiki/Ethanol "Ethanol") causes cell death at the [concentrations](/wiki/Concentration "Concentration") present in alcoholic beverages. Few cells survive a one-hour exposure to 5–10% ethanol or a 15-second exposure to 30–40% ethanol in cell culture, where surviving cells might undergo genomic changes leading to carcinogenesis. But recent evidence suggests that the cytotoxic effect of ethanol on the cells lining the oral cavity, pharynx and esophagus activates the division of the stem cells located in deeper layers of the mucosa to replace the dead cells.

Every time stem cells divide, they become exposed to unavoidable errors associated with cell division (e.g., mutations arising during [DNA replication](/wiki/DNA_replication "DNA replication") and chromosomal alterations occurring during mitosis) and also become highly vulnerable to the genotoxic activity of DNA-damaging agents (e.g., acetaldehyde and tobacco carcinogens). Alcohol consumption probably increases the risk of developing cancer of the oral cavity, pharynx and esophagus by promoting the accumulation of cell divisions in the stem cells that maintain these tissues in homeostasis. Located on the foreshore of [Sydney Harbour](/wiki/Sydney_Harbour "Sydney Harbour"), it is widely regarded as one of the world's most famous and distinctive buildings, and a masterpiece of 20th-century architecture.[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4)

Designed by Danish architect [Jørn Utzon](/wiki/J%C3%B8rn_Utzon "Jørn Utzon") and completed by an Australian architectural team headed by [Peter Hall](/wiki/Peter_Hall_(architect) "Peter Hall (architect)"), the building was formally opened by [Queen Elizabeth II](/wiki/Elizabeth_II "Elizabeth II") on 20 October 1973,[[5]](#cite_note-opened-5) 16 years after Utzon's 1957 selection as winner of an international design competition. The [Government of New South Wales](/wiki/Government_of_New_South_Wales "Government of New South Wales"), led by the [premier](/wiki/Premier_of_New_South_Wales "Premier of New South Wales"), [Joseph Cahill](/wiki/Joseph_Cahill "Joseph Cahill"), authorised work to begin in 1958 with Utzon directing construction. The government's decision to build Utzon's design is often overshadowed by circumstances that followed, including cost and scheduling overruns as well as the architect's ultimate resignation.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

The building and its surrounds occupy the whole of [Bennelong Point](/wiki/Bennelong_Point "Bennelong Point") on [Sydney Harbour](/wiki/Port_Jackson "Port Jackson"), between [Sydney Cove](/wiki/Sydney_Cove "Sydney Cove") and [Farm Cove](/wiki/Farm_Cove,_New_South_Wales "Farm Cove, New South Wales"), adjacent to the [Sydney central business district](/wiki/Sydney_central_business_district "Sydney central business district") and the [Royal Botanic Garden](/wiki/Royal_Botanic_Garden,_Sydney "Royal Botanic Garden, Sydney"), and near to the [Sydney Harbour Bridge](/wiki/Sydney_Harbour_Bridge "Sydney Harbour Bridge").
